commits.author: Giulio Ardoino
commits.subject: docs: render both README screenshots at the same size
commits.body:
The two screenshots are the same 1220x2712, but the README showed the
right one about 3.5% smaller. GitHub sizes markdown table columns from
their content, and "Sessions" is a wider heading than "Detail", so its
column took 418px against 404px and each bare image scaled to fill
whichever column it landed in.

Pinning the two columns to 50% is what actually fixes it. A fixed width
on the images equalises the desktop view but not a phone: GitHub's
max-width: 100% still clamps each image to its own unequal cell, which
put them 13px apart again at a 420px viewport. Explicit columns hold at
every width, and the images keep scaling down responsively inside them.

Both also gain the alt text that the bare ![]() form never had.

commits.author: Giulio Ardoino
commits.subject: ci: credit contributors in release notes instead of the merge
commits.body:
generate_release_notes listed one line per pull request, each ending in
"by @<whoever merged it>". On this repo that is almost always the
maintainer, so the notes read as though the maintainer wrote the desktop
layout and everything else, and the people who actually contributed
appeared as two lines among ten.

CI cannot tell a contribution from the merge that landed it, so it no
longer guesses. The annotated tag message — already written by hand at
release time, and already carrying a credits line in v2.2.0 and v2.3.0 —
becomes the release body, with the build notes and a full changelog link
appended for anyone who wants commit-level detail.

Checkout needs full history for this: the tag annotation and the previous
tag are both absent from a depth-1 clone. A tag with no annotation body
yields a terse release rather than a failed one.

CONTRIBUTING gains a "Cutting a release" section stating the convention,
since it is now a judgement call rather than something the tooling does.

+## Cutting a release
+
+Bump `version` in `web/package.json`, commit it as `chore: release vX.Y.Z`, then tag that commit and
+push both. Everything else — the version code, the Android metadata, the signed APK, the GitHub
+release — is derived from that one field by CI.
+
+```bash
+git tag -a v2.4.0 -F release-notes.txt
+git push origin main && git push origin v2.4.0
+```
+
+**The tag annotation is the release notes.** CI publishes its body verbatim, so write it for someone
+deciding whether to update: what changed, then who to thank.
+
+**Credit contributors, not the merge.** GitHub's generated notes are switched off deliberately. They
+list one line per pull request attributed to whoever pressed merge, which on this repo means the
+maintainer collects credit for work other people did. So do not enumerate pull requests or say who
+did what task by task. Name the people whose work is in the release, say what they contributed, and
+give the largest contribution a `Special thanks`. Anyone who wants commit-level detail has the full
+changelog link that CI appends.
+

commits.subject: docs: spell out the release notes format, bullets included
commits.body:
The convention said what to leave out and not what the notes look like, so
the first pass at it replaced the changelog bullets with prose paragraphs.
Only the "by @someone in <pull request>" tail was ever the problem: the
bullet list itself is the format we want, for the changes and for the
credits.

Gives the section a template of the two headings CI wraps, so the next
release does not have to infer the shape from a rule about attribution.
